etymology: From Greek Aithiops (G128, 'burnt-face,' an Ethiopian) and eunouchos (G2135, a chamberlain or castrated court official); the man of Acts 8 was a high treasurer under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians.
biblical_def: The Ethiopian eunuch of Acts 8:26-39 is one of the great trophies of sovereign grace recorded in the early church, a man of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians who had charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship and was returning home reading the prophet Isaiah aloud in his chariot. The Spirit of God so ordered providence that Philip the evangelist, divinely directed by an angel and then by the Spirit, was joined to that chariot at the very moment the eunuch read Isaiah 53, the suffering Servant led as a sheep to the slaughter. When the eunuch asked of whom the prophet spoke, Philip opened his mouth and, beginning at the same scripture, preached unto him Jesus. Here is the Reformed pattern of conversion entire: the Word read, the Word preached, the eyes opened by the Spirit, and faith confessing 'I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God' (Acts 8:37). The eunuch was baptized in water by the roadside and went on his way rejoicing. The scene typifies the gospel breaking past the boundaries of Israel toward the ends of the earth, fulfilling the promise that Ethiopia shall stretch out her hands unto God. A man once excluded from the assembly by the law (Deut 23:1) is now welcomed in Christ, who fulfills and surpasses the old barriers.
webster_summary: A high treasury official of the Ethiopian queen Candace, converted and baptized through Philip's preaching of Isaiah 53 in Acts 8.
webster_full: ETHIOPIAN EUNUCH, noun. From Greek Aithiops (G128) and eunouchos (G2135); a chamberlain over the treasure of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians.
A court official of great authority who had gone to Jerusalem to worship and was returning home reading the prophet Isaiah.
Met on the desert road by Philip the evangelist, who, beginning at Isaiah 53, preached unto him Jesus.
As it is written, 'And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God' (Acts 8:37), whereupon he was baptized.
A signal instance of the gospel reaching toward the ends of the earth and of conversion through the read and preached Word.

Act 8:38

Isa 53:7

corruption_summary: The account is sometimes reduced to a mere parable of inclusion, severing the eunuch's baptism from the confession of faith in Christ as the Son of God that the text plainly requires.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The recurring abuse is rather to read the passage as a generic celebration of welcome while ignoring its doctrinal spine. The eunuch is not received because barriers are bad; he is received because he believes that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, and that confession of Acts 8:37 is the hinge of the whole scene. Baptism follows faith; it does not replace it.

The principle to recover is that conversion in Acts is the ordinary fruit of the Word read and preached, attended by the sovereign work of the Spirit who opens blind eyes. Philip did not improvise; he began at the scripture before him and preached Jesus from Isaiah. The eunuch's joy is the joy of a sinner who has seen the suffering Servant and rested upon Him, a pattern every reader of Isaiah 53 is meant to follow.

etymology: From Greek Andreas (G406, 'manly,' from anēr, a man); the brother of Simon Peter and one of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
biblical_def: Andrew, whose name means manly, was the brother of Simon Peter and a fisherman of Bethsaida. He appears first as a disciple of John the Baptist, and when the Baptist pointed to Jesus and cried 'Behold the Lamb of God,' Andrew followed Christ and abode with Him that day (John 1:35-40). His very next act sets the pattern of his whole life: he first findeth his own brother Simon and brings him to Jesus, saying 'We have found the Messias' (John 1:41-42). Thus Peter, the great preacher of Pentecost, was brought to Christ by his quieter brother. Andrew is the apostle of bringing others to the Lord. It is Andrew who brings the lad with the five barley loaves and two small fishes to Jesus before the feeding of the five thousand (John 6:8-9), and Andrew with Philip who brings the inquiring Greeks to Christ (John 12:22). He was one of the four who heard the Olivet Discourse privately (Mark 13:3). Reformed teaching honors Andrew as a true minister of the Word in seed form, for evangelism is nothing more nor less than one sinner saying to another, come and see. His example rebukes the notion that only the prominent serve; the man who brought Peter is named with the twelve foundations of the church, an apostle of the Lamb whose labor the Lord sovereignly used to gather His elect.
webster_summary: Simon Peter's brother, one of the first disciples called, the apostle who characteristically brings others to Christ.

As it is written, 'He first findeth his own brother Simon, and saith unto him, We have found the Messias' (John 1:41).
He brought the lad with the loaves and the inquiring Greeks to Jesus, the apostle of bringing others to the Lord.

corruption_summary: Andrew is sometimes eclipsed by his more prominent brother, obscuring the biblical truth that the Lord uses obscure servants to gather the great.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger here is not redefinition but neglect; Andrew is so overshadowed by Peter that his distinct calling is easily missed. Yet Scripture names him among the twelve foundations of the church, and his quiet ministry of bringing men to Christ is the very work to which every believer is called.

The principle to recover is that the Lord delights to use the unheralded. The man who brought Peter to Jesus did more for the church than many a louder voice, for evangelism is simply one sinner saying to another, come and see. Andrew teaches that faithfulness, not prominence, is the measure of a servant, and that God's sovereign grace often works through the brother no one remembers.

etymology: From Greek huioi Skeua (G5207 + G4630); seven sons of one Sceva, a Jew and chief of the priests, who attempted to exorcise demons by the name of Jesus in Acts 19.
biblical_def: The sons of Sceva were seven Jewish exorcists, sons of a man called a chief of the priests, who appear in Acts 19:13-16 during Paul's ministry at Ephesus. Marveling at the mighty works God wrought by the hands of Paul, these vagabond exorcists presumed to take the name of the Lord Jesus and use it as a magical formula, saying over those possessed with evil spirits, 'We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth.' But the evil spirit answered, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?' and the demoniac leaped upon them, overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of the house naked and wounded. This terrifying scene teaches a doctrine the Reformed faith holds dear: the name of Jesus is not a charm to be wielded by the unbelieving, but a name that saves only those who truly trust in Him. The demons confess Christ's real authority and even know His true servant Paul, but they despise the pretender who has no living union with the Lord. Christ's power over the powers of darkness is real, but it is exercised through faith, not magic. The episode produced great fear, the magnifying of the name of the Lord Jesus, and the public burning of books of curious arts worth fifty thousand pieces of silver. It stands as a permanent rebuke to every superstitious abuse of holy things and to the presumption that the gospel can be borrowed without the new birth.
webster_summary: Seven Jewish would-be exorcists, sons of a chief priest, overpowered by a demon when they tried to use the name of Jesus as a magic charm.
webster_full: SONS OF SCEVA, noun. From Greek huioi Skeua (G5207 + G4630); seven sons of Sceva, a Jew and chief of the priests at Ephesus.

As it is written, 'And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded' (Acts 19:16).
A standing warning that the name of Jesus is no charm for the unbelieving but saves only the truly faithful.

And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.
corruption_summary: The passage is misused by sensationalists who treat the name of Jesus as a power-formula, the very error the sons of Sceva committed and were judged for.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The abuse is older and more practical: deliverance ministries and superstitious practice that treat the name of Jesus as an incantation, repeating it as though syllables carried power apart from living faith. The sons of Sceva are the Bible's own refutation of such magic; the demon mocked them precisely because they had the formula without the faith.

The principle to recover is that Christ's authority over demons is genuine and that the unseen war is real, yet that authority is never transferable to the unconverted. Only those united to Christ by faith stand in His power. The name of Jesus saves the believer and terrifies the demon, but in the mouth of a stranger to grace it brings only shame, as Ephesus learned to its great fear and to the magnifying of the Lord.

etymology: From Greek deō (G1210, to bind) and ho ischuros (G2478, the strong one); Christ's parable of binding the strong man before spoiling his house (Matt 12:29; Mark 3:27).
biblical_def: Binding the strong man is the Lord Jesus' own parabolic explanation of His authority over Satan, given in answer to the blasphemous charge that He cast out devils by Beelzebub. Christ asks, 'how can one enter into a strong man's house, and spoil his goods, except he first bind the strong man? and then he will spoil his house' (Matt 12:29). The strong man is Satan; his house is his dominion over fallen men; his goods are the souls held captive at his will. The fact that Christ casts out demons is proof that the stronger has come upon the strong, has overpowered him, taken from him all his armor wherein he trusted, and divided his spoils (Luke 11:21-22). This is the inauguration of the kingdom of God in power. The Reformed faith confesses that at the cross and in His whole earthly ministry, Christ decisively bound the strong man, leading captivity captive and spoiling principalities and powers, making a show of them openly. The binding is not the final imprisonment of the last day but the present, real, conquering authority by which the gospel now plunders Satan's kingdom, calling the elect out of darkness into light. Every conversion is a spoiling of the strong man's house. Christ alone is the stronger man, and His victory is the ground of the believer's deliverance from the power of darkness and translation into the kingdom of God's dear Son.
webster_summary: Christ's parable that He overpowers Satan, the strong man, and plunders his house, signifying the kingdom of God breaking in.
webster_full: BINDING THE STRONG MAN, noun phrase. From Greek deō (G1210) and ho ischuros (G2478); Christ's parable of overpowering Satan before spoiling his house.

The strong man is Satan; the house his dominion; the goods the souls held captive at his will.
As it is written, 'No man can enter into a strong man's house, and spoil his goods, except he will first bind the strong man; and then he will spoil his house' (Mark 3:27).
The casting out of demons proves the stronger has come, the inauguration of the kingdom of God in power.

corruption_summary: The parable is sometimes wrenched into a method for human spiritual-warfare techniques, when its sole point is the unique conquering authority of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misuse is rather a practical one: turning 'binding the strong man' into a formula or technique by which believers rebuke and bind Satan through repeated verbal commands. The text gives no such warrant; the one who binds the strong man is Christ Himself, the stronger man, and the parable is about His unique victory, not a human method.

The principle to recover is that the kingdom of God came in power when the Son of God overpowered Satan, took his armor, and divided his spoils. The believer's deliverance rests entirely upon Christ's accomplished triumph at Calvary, where He spoiled principalities and powers openly. We do not bind Satan; we proclaim the One who already has, and every conversion is a soul plundered from the strong man's house.

etymology: From Greek ekballō (G1544, to cast out) and daimonion (G1140, a demon or evil spirit); the exorcising of unclean spirits by the authority of Christ in the Gospels.
biblical_def: Casting out demons describes the authoritative expulsion of unclean spirits by the Lord Jesus and, by His commission, His apostles. Throughout the Gospels Christ rebukes demons and they obey Him instantly, for He commands them with authority and power (Luke 4:36). Unlike the elaborate rituals of pagan and Jewish exorcists, Christ casts out spirits with a word, and even the demons confess Him to be the Holy One of God and the Son of the Most High. The Reformed faith affirms that this authority is a sign that the kingdom of God is come: 'if I cast out devils by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God is come unto you' (Matt 12:28). The reality of the unseen war is not myth but the sober teaching of Scripture; there are fallen angels under Satan, real and personal, who afflict and oppress, and Christ is their conqueror. Yet the Bible carefully restrains sensationalism. Christ rejoiced not chiefly that the spirits were subject to His disciples, but that their names were written in heaven (Luke 10:20). The greater wonder is salvation, not spectacle. With the close of the apostolic age the sign-gifts ceased, and the church today resists both the unbelief that denies the demonic and the showmanship that turns deliverance into a stage. The believer stands in the finished victory of Christ, who through death destroyed him that had the power of death, that is, the devil, and delivers His people from bondage.
webster_summary: The authoritative expulsion of unclean spirits by Christ, a sign of the present kingdom of God and of His conquest of Satan.

corruption_summary: The subject is corrupted both by modern unbelief that denies the demonic and by sensationalists who turn deliverance into showmanship.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The twofold abuse is older and plainer. On one side, a rationalist temper reduces the demoniacs of the Gospels to mere mental illness, denying the personal reality of fallen spirits that Scripture everywhere assumes. On the other side, sensational deliverance ministries manufacture spectacle, presuming powers the apostolic age possessed as signs that have since ceased.

The principle to recover is the sobriety of Christ Himself, who bid His disciples rejoice not that the spirits were subject to them but that their names were written in heaven. The unseen war is real; Christ's authority over it is total; and the believer rests in His finished triumph at the cross rather than seeking signs. Salvation, not spectacle, is the great wonder, and the conquered devil flees before the gospel of grace.

etymology: From Greek stephanos ex akanthōn (G4735 + G173); the plaited crown of thorns the soldiers pressed upon the head of Christ in mockery (John 19:2).
biblical_def: The crown of thorns is the cruel diadem the Roman soldiers platted and set upon the head of Jesus, arraying Him in a purple robe and saluting Him in mockery as King of the Jews (John 19:2; Matt 27:29). What the soldiers intended as derision the providence of God made into profound truth, for the One they crowned in scorn is indeed the King of kings. The Reformed faith sees here a rich typology rooted in Genesis. When Adam fell, the ground was cursed for his sake, and the LORD said, 'thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee' (Gen 3:18). The thorn is the very emblem of the curse that came upon creation through sin. Now the last Adam, the Lord from heaven, takes that curse upon His own brow; the sign of Eden's judgment is pressed into the flesh of the Redeemer. He who knew no sin is made a curse for us, for it is written, 'Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree' (Gal 3:13). The crown of thorns thus preaches penal substitution in a single image: the curse of the ground gathered up and borne by Christ, that His people might receive the crown of life. He is crowned in mockery and yet crowned in truth, a King reigning from a tree, who through suffering entered into His glory and will at the last be crowned with many crowns.
webster_summary: The plaited crown of thorns set on Christ's head in mockery, bearing the curse of the ground (Gen 3:18) for His people.

corruption_summary: The crown of thorns is sometimes reduced to a mere symbol of generic suffering, severing it from the curse of the ground and the doctrine of substitution.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The recurring loss is the typological emptying of the image, treating the crown of thorns as a moving emblem of pain or injustice while severing it from the curse of Genesis 3 and the substitutionary atonement it preaches. Sentiment without doctrine cannot bear the weight of this crown.

The principle to recover is that the thorn is the very token of the curse pronounced upon the ground, and that Christ wore it upon His brow because He was being made a curse for His people. The crown of thorns is penal substitution in a single picture: the King takes the curse of Eden so that His redeemed may receive the unfading crown of life. To grasp the thorns rightly is to behold Calvary.

etymology: From Greek klasis tou artou (G2800 + G740); the breaking of bread practiced by the early church, embracing both common fellowship meals and the Lord's Supper (Acts 2:42, 46).
biblical_def: The breaking of bread is the apostolic expression that describes the fellowship of the early church gathered around the table, embracing both their common meals and, preeminently, the Lord's Supper instituted by Christ. After Pentecost the new believers continued steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers (Acts 2:42). Daily they continued with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart (Acts 2:46). The Reformed faith confesses the Lord's Supper as one of the two ordinances Christ appointed for His church, in which the bread broken sets forth His body given and the cup His blood shed for the remission of sins. It is no bare memorial only, but a true communion of the body and blood of Christ, received by faith, in which believers feed upon Him spiritually and are knit together as one bread, one body (1 Cor 10:16-17). The breaking of bread therefore signifies both vertical communion with the crucified and risen Lord and horizontal communion among His people. The 1689 Confession teaches that worthy receivers, outwardly partaking of the visible elements, do also inwardly by faith receive and feed upon Christ crucified. Thus the early church's breaking of bread, marked by gladness and singleness of heart, is the abiding pattern of a people gathered in word, sacrament, and prayer.
webster_summary: The early church's table fellowship, embracing common meals and especially the Lord's Supper, a communion of the body of Christ.

corruption_summary: The breaking of bread is corrupted by reducing the Lord's Supper to a bare memorial or, oppositely, to a transubstantiated sacrifice, both departing from the Reformed confession.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The historic corruptions are doctrinal and remain. On one hand the supper has been made a propitiatory sacrifice in which the bread is supposed to become the literal flesh of Christ, robbing the once-for-all offering of Calvary of its sufficiency. On the other hand it has been reduced to a bare mental memorial, an empty sign emptied of all spiritual feeding.

The principle to recover is the Reformed and confessional middle, held by the 1689: the supper is no new sacrifice, yet no bare memorial either, but a true spiritual communion in which worthy receivers, by faith, feed upon Christ crucified. The bread broken proclaims His body given for sinners, and the fellowship of the table binds the church into one body until He come.

roots_lines: Greek klasis (G2800) — a breaking, used of the breaking of bread at the table
Greek artos (G740) — bread, a loaf; the element broken in fellowship and the supper
Greek koinōnia (G2842) — communion, fellowship, the sharing of the one bread
Greek klaō (G2806) — to break, the verb Christ used when He brake the bread
Acts 2:42 binds breaking of bread to doctrine, fellowship, and prayer in one ordered worship
usage: The breaking of bread united the early church in worship, word, and prayer.
In the supper the bread broken proclaims Christ's body given for His people.
The breaking of bread is communion both with the risen Lord and among His saints.

etymology: From Hebrew mabbul (H3999, a flood, deluge) and the name Noach (H5146, rest); the worldwide deluge of Genesis 6-9 by which God judged the earth.
biblical_def: The flood of Noah is the historical, worldwide deluge by which the LORD judged a world grown wholly corrupt and violent, while sovereignly preserving eight souls in the ark He commanded Noah to build (Gen 6-9). The Reformed faith receives the account as true history, not legend, for our Lord Jesus Christ Himself appealed to the days of Noah as a real and coming pattern of judgment (Matt 24:37-39), and the apostle Peter twice grounds doctrine upon it as literal fact. God saw that the wickedness of man was great and that every imagination of his heart was only evil continually, a stark testimony to total depravity. Yet Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD, and being warned of God moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house, by which faith he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith (Heb 11:7). The flood is rich in typology. Peter teaches that the eight souls saved by water are the figure of baptism (1 Pet 3:20-21), the waters of judgment becoming the waters of salvation for those in the ark, even as the believer is saved through union with the death and resurrection of Christ. Peter further teaches that as the old world perished by water, so the present heavens and earth are reserved unto fire against the day of judgment (2 Pet 3:5-7). The flood thus preaches both the certainty of final judgment and the safety of all hidden in Christ, the true ark.
webster_summary: The historical worldwide deluge of Genesis 6-9 by which God judged the world and saved eight souls in the ark, a type of baptism and final judgment.
webster_full: FLOOD OF NOAH, noun. From Hebrew mabbul (H3999, a deluge) and Noach (H5146, rest); the worldwide flood of Genesis 6-9.
A true and universal judgment upon a world grown corrupt and filled with violence.
Eight souls were saved in the ark, the figure of baptism according to the apostle Peter.
As it is written, 'By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house' (Heb 11:7).
The old world perished by water; the present world is reserved unto fire against the day of judgment.
scriptures: Gen 6:5
And God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.
Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water.
Whereby the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished:
Heb 11:7

By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house; by the which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith.
corruption_summary: The flood is corrupted when treated as mere myth or as a local event, denying the worldwide judgment our Lord and His apostles affirmed as history.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The longstanding assault is to demote the flood from history to folklore, or to shrink it to a local Mesopotamian inundation. But the Lord Jesus appealed to the days of Noah as a real and coming reality, and Peter grounds the certainty of final judgment upon the literal fact that the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished.

The principle to recover is the unity of judgment and salvation in the flood. The waters that drowned the rebellious world bore the ark and its eight souls to safety, which Peter names the figure of baptism. As surely as the flood came, fire is reserved for the present heavens and earth, and the only safety in either is to be hidden in Christ, the true ark, by the righteousness which is by faith.
roots_summary: Hebrew mabbul (H3999) and Noach (H5146) name the deluge and the man through whom God preserved eight souls.
roots_lines: Hebrew mabbul (H3999) — the flood, the deluge, used uniquely of Noah's waters
Hebrew Noach (H5146) — Noah, 'rest' or 'comfort,' the preacher of righteousness
Hebrew tebah (H8392) — the ark, the vessel of salvation through the waters
Greek kataklusmos (G2627) — cataclysm, the New Testament term for the flood (Matt 24:38)
The eight souls saved by water are the figure of baptism and a type of final judgment by fire
usage: The flood of Noah was a true worldwide judgment, as the Lord Jesus Himself affirmed.
Eight souls were saved through the waters, the figure of baptism and the safety of the ark.
As the old world perished by water, the present world is reserved unto fire.

etymology: From Greek tuphloō (G5186, to blind) and pneumatikos (G4152, spiritual); the inability of the natural man to perceive and receive the things of the Spirit of God.
biblical_def: Spiritual blindness is the settled incapacity of the natural, unregenerate man to perceive, understand, and embrace the things of God. The Reformed faith roots this doctrine in total depravity: the fall has not merely wounded man but darkened his understanding, so that the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness unto him, neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned (1 Cor 2:14). This blindness is moral and judicial, not a mere lack of information. The god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ should shine unto them (2 Cor 4:4). The man born blind in John 9 is a living parable of this truth: Christ gives him sight while the seeing Pharisees remain blind, and the Lord declares that for judgment He is come, that they which see not might see, and that they which see might be made blind (John 9:39). Because the bondage is total, the remedy can only be sovereign and supernatural. No argument or moral effort can open blind eyes; only the new birth, the God who commanded light to shine out of darkness shining in the heart, gives the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6). Spiritual sight is therefore the gift of monergistic grace, and every believer who now sees does so because the Lord opened eyes once shut fast.
webster_summary: The natural man's settled inability to perceive the things of God, cured only by the sovereign gift of the new birth.
webster_full: SPIRITUAL BLINDNESS, noun. From Greek tuphloō (G5186, to blind) and pneumatikos (G4152, spiritual); the incapacity of the natural man to discern divine things.
A moral and judicial darkness, not a mere want of information, rooted in the fall.
The god of this world blinds the minds of unbelievers lest the gospel light shine unto them.
As it is written, 'But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him' (1 Cor 2:14).
Cured only by the new birth, when God who commanded light to shine out of darkness shines in the heart.
scriptures: But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them.
Joh 9:39
And Jesus said, For judgment I am come into this world, that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind.
For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: Spiritual blindness is corrupted when softened into mere ignorance curable by education or persuasion, denying the totality of the natural man's inability.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The persistent error is doctrinal: to recast spiritual blindness as a curable ignorance that the right argument, experience, or program might overcome, leaving the sinner with some native power to choose the light. This denies the plain word that the natural man cannot know the things of God, for they are spiritually discerned.

The principle to recover is total depravity and the monergistic remedy that follows from it. Because the blindness is total and judicial, the cure must be wholly of God, the same Creator who said let there be light shining anew in the darkened heart. Spiritual sight is not coaxed from the sinner but given in the new birth, and every soul that now beholds the glory of God in the face of Christ does so by sovereign grace alone.
roots_summary: Greek tuphloō (G5186) and related terms describe the darkening of the natural man's mind to the things of God.
roots_lines: Greek tuphloō (G5186) — to make blind, used of Satan blinding unbelieving minds
Greek tuphlos (G5185) — blind; the man born blind of John 9 a parable of the soul
Greek psuchikos (G5591) — natural, soulish; the man without the Spirit who cannot discern
Greek pōroō (G4456) — to harden, to make callous, the kindred blinding of the heart
Only palingenesia (G3824), the new birth, gives the blind soul spiritual sight
usage: Spiritual blindness is total: the natural man cannot know the things of the Spirit.
No argument cures spiritual blindness; only the God of creation shining in the heart.
The man born blind in John 9 pictures the soul to whom Christ alone gives sight.

etymology: From Greek pulai hadou (G4439 + G86); the gates of Hades, the powers of death, which Christ declares shall not prevail against His church (Matt 16:18).
biblical_def: The gates of hell is the phrase the Lord Jesus used in His great promise concerning the church: 'upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it' (Matt 16:18). The word rendered hell is hades, the realm of death, and gates in Scripture signify both the strength of a city and the seat of its counsel and power. The gates of hell therefore are the assembled powers of death and darkness, all the strength of Satan's kingdom marshaled against the people of God. Christ's promise is twofold and absolute. First, He Himself will build His church; it is His own work, founded upon the confession that He is the Christ, the Son of the living God, the rock upon which the whole edifice stands. Second, the powers of death shall not prevail, shall not overpower or outlast it. The Reformed faith confesses the perseverance and final preservation of the church catholic against every assault of hell, persecution, heresy, and the grave itself. Because Christ has Himself passed through death and risen, holding the keys of hell and of death (Rev 1:18), the gates of the grave cannot hold His body the church. This is no promise that the church will escape conflict; it is the promise that in the conflict she cannot be destroyed, for her Builder is the risen Lord whose victory over the powers is already won and forever sure.
webster_summary: The powers of death and darkness which, by Christ's promise in Matt 16:18, can never prevail against the church He builds.
webster_full: GATES OF HELL, noun phrase. From Greek pulai hadou (G4439 + G86); the gates of Hades, the powers of death arrayed against the church.
Gates in Scripture signify the strength and the counsel of a city; here the marshaled might of Satan's kingdom.
Christ promises both to build His church and to preserve it against every assault of death.
As it is written, 'Upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it' (Matt 16:18).
Her Builder is the risen Lord who holds the keys of hell and of death, so the grave cannot hold her.
scriptures: And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.
Rev 1:18
I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death.
Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
corruption_summary: The promise is corrupted when the rock is made to be Peter and his successors, or when the verse is wrenched into a charter for human triumphalism rather than Christ's preserving work.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The historic corruption is the claim that the rock is the person of Peter and a line of successors, founding the church on a man rather than on the confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. Scripture elsewhere names Christ Himself the foundation and the apostles and prophets together the foundation under Him, with Christ the chief corner stone.

The principle to recover is that the promise is Christ-centered from end to end. He builds; He preserves; the gates of death cannot prevail because He has Himself conquered death and holds its keys. The verse is not a charter for human power or earthly triumph but the believer's assurance that the church, founded on Christ and indwelt by His Spirit, will outlast the grave and every power of hell.
roots_summary: Greek pulai (G4439) and hadēs (G86) together name the powers of death that cannot overcome Christ's church.
roots_lines: Greek pulē (G4439) — a gate, a figure for the strength and counsel of a city
Greek hadēs (G86) — Hades, the realm of death, rendered 'hell' in the KJV
Greek katischuō (G2729) — to prevail against, to overpower; what the gates cannot do
Greek petra (G4073) — the rock, the confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God
Greek ekklēsia (G1577) — the church, the assembly Christ Himself builds and preserves
usage: Christ promised that the gates of hell shall not prevail against His church.
The rock is the confession that Jesus is the Christ, not the person of any man.
Because Christ holds the keys of death, the gates of hell cannot hold His church.
